title: Where does the tray balance?
allegory: A point on a triangle is the balance point of a weightless tray with one kilo of sand shared between its three corners; the point is on the tray exactly when no corner needs negative sand.
map: one kilo of sand shared between three corners
three weights that always sum to one: w + u + v = 1
how much sand sits on corner A, B and C
the weights w = 1 − u − v, u and v
the spot where the tray balances on a fingertip

a helium balloon tied to a corner (negative sand)

chapters.name: Hit or miss?
chapters.note: did that ray go through, or past the edge?

cap.1: You fire rays at a triangle and need a yes or no for each one: did it pass through the triangle, or sail past an edge?
cap.2: triangle_ray_intersects must answer hit or miss for one ray and one triangle. Later you run it for every ray at once, so the test has to be pure arithmetic.
cap.3: Ray-triangle intersection reduces to a point-in-triangle test on the plane hit point. We want a test that is a few comparisons on the output of one linear solve.

cap.1: Share one kilo of sand between the three corners of a weightless tray. The spot where it balances on a fingertip is a blend of the corners.
cap.2: Those three shares are barycentric coordinates. Any point on the triangle's plane is one blend wA + uB + vC, and the shares always add up to one.
cap.3: P = wA + uB + vC with w + u + v = 1 is an affine combination; every point on the plane has exactly one such (w, u, v). Barycentre means centre of mass.

parts.note: u of the way to B
v of the way to C

cap.1: Where the ray lands on the tray's plane can be written two ways: some steps along the ray, or a blend of the corners. Set them equal and solve.
cap.2: Move the unknowns left: −sD + u(B−A) + v(C−A) = O − A. That is a 3x3 system. Stack −D, B−A, C−A as columns and solve once for s, u and v.
cap.3: Solve [−D, B−A, C−A]·(s, u, v) = O − A. Accept when u ≥ 0, v ≥ 0, u + v ≤ 1. Batched over rays it is a single t.linalg.solve call.

cap.1: Slide the balance point from corner A towards the far edge. A's share of sand shrinks. The moment it goes below zero, you have left the tray.
cap.2: Along this path the three weights still add to one at every step. Only the sign of A's weight changes as you cross edge BC, so the sign is the whole test.
cap.3: Each coordinate is an affine function that vanishes on the opposite edge. Crossing BC flips sign(w); the constraint w + u + v = 1 holds throughout.

chapters.name: The sideways ray
chapters.note: parallel ray: no answer to find

cap.1: A ray running parallel to the tray never lands on it. There is nothing to solve for, so call it a miss instead of letting the maths fall over.
cap.2: A parallel ray makes the 3x3 matrix singular and the solver cannot give one answer. Check the determinant first and mark those rays as misses.
cap.3: Parallel rays give det = 0. The batched fix: mask |det| < 1e-8, substitute the identity so the solve runs, then force those rays to False.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Batch it over every ray at once in raytrace_mesh
Softmax weights: never negative, always sum to one
Attention output = a balance point of value vectors

cap.1: Weights that are never negative and add to one come back all the time. Softmax makes exactly those, so attention's output is a balance point too.
cap.2: An attention head blends value vectors with softmax weights. Like the tray, its output can never land outside the region those vectors span.
cap.3: Softmax outputs are convex weights, so each head's output lies in the convex hull of its value vectors: a useful bound when you read or steer what a head writes.

coda.title: Move the hit point with u and v; watch the three corner weights

readouts.label: inside the triangle?
readouts.f: (u >= -0.0001 && v >= -0.0001 && u + v <= 1.0001) ? 'yes: all three weights >= 0' : 'no: a weight went negative'

caption.1: Drag u and v. The sum readout never changes. Push u + v past 1 and A's bar dips below zero: the point has slipped off the tray.
caption.2: Try u = 0.7, v = 0.5. The sum is still 1, but A's weight is −0.2, so it is a miss. Summing proves nothing; the signs decide.
caption.3: w = 1 − u − v makes the sum identically 1. The inside test is the three half-planes u ≥ 0, v ≥ 0, w ≥ 0, one per edge.

where_else: Softmax outputs: non-negative weights summing to one, so attention returns a point inside the hull of its value vectors
GPUs blending colours and textures stored at the corners of every rendered triangle
A probability distribution over three outcomes is a point on a triangle
Linear interpolation is the two-corner version, with weights (1 − t, t)

hamming.what: Three weights that say how much of each corner a point is made of, and the point is inside exactly when none is negative.
hamming.when: Whenever you need to know whether a point lies inside a triangle, or to blend values stored at a triangle's corners.
hamming.why: It turns a geometry question into sign checks on the output of one small linear solve, which batches over millions of rays.

object.title: The balance tent
object.subtitle: Three ramps, one per corner; the triangle is where all of them stay above the floor.
object.f: show < 0.5 ? 1 - x - y : show < 1.5 ? x : show < 2.5 ? y : min(min(1 - x - y, x), y)

knobs.label: Weight on A, B, C, or the smallest

cap.1: This ramp is the weight on corner A. It is 1 at A and slopes down to 0 along the far edge.
cap.2: Height = w = 1 − u − v over the (u, v) floor. A tilted plane: 1 at A, 0 on edge BC, negative beyond it.
cap.3: w(u, v) = 1 − u − v is affine and its zero set is line BC. Each coordinate is an affine function vanishing on the opposite edge.

cap.1: Corner B has its own ramp: 1 at B, 0 along the edge facing it.
cap.2: Height = u: 1 at B, 0 along edge AC. Corner C's ramp (height v) is the same shape turned.
cap.3: u and v are the coordinate functions themselves; together with w they form a partition of unity over the plane.

cap.1: Keep only the smallest of the three weights at every spot. You get a tent, and the part above the floor is exactly the triangle.
cap.2: Height = min(w, u, v). It is ≥ 0 exactly inside the triangle, so 'inside?' is 'is the smallest weight ≥ 0?'.
cap.3: min of three affine functions is concave and piecewise linear; its non-negative superlevel set is the triangle, the intersection of three half-planes.

cap.1: The peak sits where all three weights are equal, one third each. Walk off any edge and the tent dips under the floor.
cap.2: The maximum of min(w, u, v) is 1/3, at the centroid. Each slope of the tent belongs to whichever weight is smallest there.
cap.3: The maximum is at the centroid, height 1/3; the ridges are where two coordinates tie for smallest.

cap.1: Softmax weights live on this same kind of tent: never negative, always adding to one.
cap.2: Any weights that are non-negative and sum to one pick a point inside the shape their corners make: softmax, mixtures, attention.
cap.3: The triangle is the 2-simplex. Softmax maps logits onto the (n−1)-simplex, which is why attention outputs are convex combinations.

predict.q: A hit point has weights (0.5, 0.7, −0.2). Inside or outside the triangle?

options.t: Inside: the weights sum to one

predict.why: Every point on the plane has weights summing to one. Only the signs separate inside from outside.

predict.q: The test checks u ≥ 0, v ≥ 0 and u + v ≤ 1. Where is the check on the third weight?

options.t: It is u + v ≤ 1, because w = 1 − u − v
Triangles only need two weights checked

predict.why: w ≥ 0 and u + v ≤ 1 are the same statement written two ways.

options.t: At the centre, where all three weights are 1/3

predict.why: At a corner two weights are zero. The smallest weight is as big as it can be when all three are equal.

object.where: Anywhere weights are non-negative and sum to one: softmax, attention, colour blending across triangles.
